evidence_level: A for the tutoring model; at-scale size lower
pathway: Tutoring by paid or stipended, trained tutors using a structured math curriculum raises standardized math scores; the gain shrinks at scale and volunteer-only math tutoring has not shown it.
model_match: School-day (or school-integrated) math tutoring by paid or stipended trained tutors (teachers, paraprofessionals, AmeriCorps members) using a structured math curriculum, about 90 minutes or more a week, one-to-one or groups of two to four. Volunteer-only math tutoring gets no evidence level from this link.
typical_effect: Plan on 0 to 0.10 SD on the state math test when a district or partner scales tutoring quickly; 0.15 to 0.25 SD on broad standardized math tests for well-run structured programs.
caveats: A large district-run tutoring program (Nashville, over 6,800 students) moved reading but not math. In an eight-district recovery study, only one of 12 math programs showed a robust effect. The volunteer-tutoring meta-analysis found reading-subskill gains but no significant math gain. Drop 'volunteer tutoring counts only with a smaller expected gain' for math.
rationale: Scale nulls and the volunteer null bound the pooled 0.27 SD; the math-specific evidence argues for stricter tutor and curriculum conditions than for reading.

evidence_level: B for the Math Corps model (two RCTs plus a statewide RCT)
pathway: AmeriCorps members trained to deliver a scripted math curriculum to pairs or trios of grade 4-8 students raise broad standardized math scores.
model_match: Math Corps model: stipended AmeriCorps tutors, scripted evidence-based math curriculum, pairs or groups of three, 30-45 minute sessions totalling about 90 minutes a week, tutor training and coaching, grades 4-8.
typical_effect: Intent-to-treat d = 0.17 (d = 0.24 at intended dosage) and g = 0.17 to 0.22 on STAR Math; state test (Minnesota MCA) g = 0.06, not significant.
caveats: The only state-test estimate (statewide RCT) was small and not significant; the STAR gains are on a district interim test. One developer organization. The dosage (about 90 minutes a week) is below the L-02 'three sessions a week' condition, so state the condition in minutes. A matched-comparison Mathematica study and a GO Tutor Corps QED (+0.10, grades 6-10) are supporting leads only.
rationale: This is the partner-runnable, nonprofit-operated math tutoring model with the most replicated randomized evidence in grades 4-8; it is close to the City Year and AmeriCorps structures Philadelphia partners already use.

evidence_level: B for structured early-grade math intervention protocols (standardized tests, not the state test)
pathway: Scripted small-group or one-to-one math intervention protocols delivered during the school day to low-achieving students in grades 1-4 raise standardized math scores.
model_match: A named, validated math intervention protocol (for example Number Rockets, Pirate Math, Fraction Face-Off!, ROOTS) delivered by trained tutors or paraprofessionals to students below grade level, about 30 or more hours a year, during the school day.
typical_effect: Number Rockets scale-up replication (76 schools, 994 first graders) about 0.34 on TEMA-3; ROOTS +0.19 across five studies; Pirate Math (grade 3) +0.37; Fraction Face-Off! (grade 4) +0.51 on the qualifying measure.
caveats: Outcomes are norm-referenced math tests (TEMA-3, KeyMath, WJ), not the PSSA; most studies are grade 1 or grade 4, so the grade 3 state test is inferred. Many were run by research teams in Nashville and Houston. The Number Rockets result is a true at-scale replication, which is why this reaches B. The Campbell and RER meta-analyses place tutoring and small-group instruction among the largest effects for low-SES and at-risk students.
rationale: Gives L-02 a curriculum condition and grade-3-relevant evidence; partners running school-day intervention blocks can adopt a named protocol at low cost (materials are free or inexpensive).

pathway: Daily in-school math tutoring in grades 9-10 raises high school math test scores, including a cheaper version that alternates tutor time with software.
model_match: Saga-style daily school-day math tutoring in grades 9-10: 2-to-1 with a paid tutor, or the tested 4-to-1 version in which two students work with the tutor and two on computer-assisted learning, alternating daily.
typical_effect: Technology-blended version: 0.23 SD on math standardized tests for participants at about 30% lower cost per pupil; Evidence for ESSA mean +0.14 across three RCTs (confirm whether intent-to-treat).
caveats: Still one program in Chicago and one other large district; the test is not the Keystone. A second high school model (daily tutorials at MATCH charter high school, Kraft 2015) raised ELA but found no average math effect, so the math gain is not automatic for every tutoring design. The grades 7-12 Campbell review supports targeted small-group math instruction in general.
rationale: Adds the intent-to-treat style summary the methods reviewer could not find, a lower-cost replication, and a high-school null that keeps the model-match narrow.

pathway: An intensive summer algebra-readiness program for rising eighth graders raises algebra readiness test scores at the end of the summer.
model_match: Elevate Math model: a multi-week summer math program for rising grade 8 students, taught by credentialed math teachers with an algebra-readiness curriculum, run by a nonprofit with school districts.
typical_effect: MDTP Algebra Readiness g about 0.64-0.66; share of students rated algebra-ready rose from about 12% to 29% (end of summer).
caveats: One RCT in Silicon Valley districts; outcome measured at the end of summer only, on a readiness test rather than the Keystone or the state test; no evidence yet that the gain survives to the spring test or to Algebra I passing. Summer math effects fade elsewhere (see L-07).
rationale: The only randomized evidence on a partner-runnable summer program aimed directly at algebra; worth listing so partners know it exists and what it does not show.

pathway: Summer programs that include math raise math scores by about a tenth of a standard deviation at the end of summer, but the gain tends to fade before the spring state test.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested models: voluntary multi-week summer programs with teacher-led math; online or home-based summer math.
typical_effect: Meta-analysis of 37 experimental and quasi-experimental studies: +0.10 SD in math. BELL middle school RCT: math g = 0.06 (not significant). Online summer math with a laptop: no effect on later achievement.
caveats: Effects are usually measured in the fall; the at-scale NSLP trial shows fade-out by spring. The meta-analysis mixes designs and test types (check the share of state tests). The School District of Philadelphia's own 2021 summer report (Star Math) should be checked for design before it is cited.
rationale: Adds the newest summer-math meta-analysis and two nulls so the row states the typical size and the fade-out rather than resting on one study.

evidence_level: B (national RCT plus many state quasi-experiments pointing the same way)
pathway: 21st Century Community Learning Centers as typically run have near-zero effects on state math tests; small gains appear only among the most frequent attenders.
model_match: Not applicable: not used for credit.
typical_effect: State propensity-score evaluations: Texas center-level math and reading effects centered at d = -0.02 across 779 centers; New Jersey high vs low attenders about 0.04 SD; Rhode Island and West Virginia no significant math effect; Texas STAAR math about 4 scale-score points only at 120 or more days and negative at lower dosage.
caveats: These are matched comparisons on who chose to attend, so even the small positives at high dosage may be selection. Louisiana (Jenner & Jenner) and Indiana high-quality centers (math gain only for students failing in the fall) are the positive outliers. The Campbell review of experimental after-school evaluations found small or null academic effects. Pennsylvania's own 21st CCLC state report is descriptive pre-post with no comparison group and never qualifies. 21st CCLC does show small school-attendance gains (S1, another screener's scope).
rationale: Answers the owner's 21st CCLC question for math directly: the replicated state evidence agrees with the national null on test scores, so 21st CCLC participation earns no math credit.

pathway: Students who attend after-school programs more days score higher in math, but these comparisons follow who chooses to attend and do not show the program caused the gain.
model_match: Not applicable: not used for credit.
typical_effect: Texas 120+ days about 4 STAAR scale points, lower dosage negative; New Jersey about 0.04 SD; Philadelphia OST and 21st CCLC dosage analyses correlational.
caveats: Dosage-response claims ('our regular attenders do better on the PSSA') are the most common partner claim; they should not be made as program effects. The longitudinal Study of Promising Afterschool Programs links regular participation in high-quality programs to math gains, but the strongest quality study (NYC) found mixed signs.
rationale: Lists what partners should not claim from participation counts.

pathway: After-school program quality is associated with math gains in some longitudinal studies, but the signs are inconsistent and the high-quality-only meta-analysis shrinks the effect.
model_match: Not used for credit.
typical_effect: Mixed: regular participation in high-quality programs linked to standardized test gains (two-year study, about 3,000 students); NYC: supportive environment and structured interactions positive, 'purposeful engagement' negative.
caveats: Fewer than two independent longitudinal studies agree on the direction, so it does not meet the associated bar. Restricting the meta-analysis to high-quality studies changes the overall conclusion.
rationale: Keeps the quality row honest with the newer evidence.

pathway: Structured after-school math curricula, including software-based ones, have not raised state math scores.
model_match: Not applicable.
typical_effect: After-school ALEKS math with teacher support: Tennessee state math test g = 0.07, not significant.
caveats: Second after-school math trial pointing the same way as the national Enhanced Academic Instruction study.
rationale: Replication of the after-school math null.

pathway: Outside-provider after-school tutoring under the federal Supplemental Educational Services rule did not raise state math scores.
model_match: Not applicable.
typical_effect: Los Angeles: no significant effect on the California Standards Test in math; another large district: small, nonsignificant positive effects after five years; grade 8 after-school tutoring in New Jersey: no significant GEPA math effect.
caveats: These programs were typically low dosage (an hour or two a week), after school, with weakly trained tutors: the opposite of the L-02 conditions. Many current partner tutoring programs look like SES.
rationale: Tells partners that after-school, low-dose tutoring is the version that has failed.

pathway: The intensive multi-year after-school and summer model did not raise state math scores when it expanded to new cities.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested model: Higher Achievement.
typical_effect: Expansion RCT: state math assessment effect not significant.
caveats: Confirms the demotion of L-11: the original DC result did not replicate on the state test.
rationale: A failed replication at scale outweighs the original positive result.

pathway: A basketball-themed math game curriculum used in out-of-school or enrichment time raised math achievement compared with ordinary STEM enrichment.
model_match: NBA Math Hoops: the board game and curriculum delivered by program staff after about three hours of training, in place of other STEM enrichment time.
typical_effect: +0.19 SD versus STEM enrichment classrooms; under $20 per student beyond normal costs.
caveats: One RCT reported by the evaluator; check grades, the test (standardized or researcher-made), and whether it ran after school. No state-test outcome yet. The comparison was other enrichment, so it measures a swap of activities, which is the realistic change for partners.
rationale: A no-cost or low-cost swap that hundreds of after-school programs could make inside existing enrichment time; worth flagging even before replication.

pathway: Out-of-school STEM enrichment (robotics, apprenticeships, project-based clubs) has not shown reliable gains on state math tests.
model_match: Not applicable.
typical_effect: Baltimore summer robotics: state math not significant. One i3 QED of extended-learning STEM in Tennessee: TNReady math g = 0.40 (unreplicated).
caveats: The Abt Citizen Schools study compared STEM apprenticeships with other apprenticeships, so it is not a program-vs-no-program test and should not be cited for math. The CrimeSolutions profile for Citizen Schools is the program-level check. The single large positive QED needs replication before any credit.
rationale: Partners often claim STEM enrichment raises math scores; the evidence does not support it yet.

pathway: Universal free meals raise elementary math scores slightly in some states; breakfast-in-the-classroom and breakfast-after-the-bell show no test gains.
model_match: Not applicable.
typical_effect: Community Eligibility in South Carolina: about +0.06 SD elementary math; multilingual learners +0.03 math; NYC breakfast in the classroom: no gains; Arkansas breakfast after the bell (grade 3): no meaningful effect; school breakfast availability (RD): positive.
caveats: Philadelphia already has universal meals under the Community Eligibility Provision, so the expansion results do not describe a partner lever. Food programs timed to the end of the SNAP month have a mechanism (scores dip late in the benefit cycle) but no program trial.
rationale: Adds the math-specific meal studies the owner asked for and states why none gives partner credit.

pathway: More family income raises young children's achievement a little; earnings gains from minimum wage increases did not.
model_match: Not used for credit. Tested change: household income increases from welfare-to-work earnings supplements or tax credits.
typical_effect: About 5-6% of an SD per $1,000 a year for young children (random-assignment welfare experiments); minimum-wage earnings changes: little effect.
caveats: A partner benefits-access program delivers a few hundred dollars, implying about 0.01 SD. The young-child estimates are mostly below grade 3.
rationale: Second independent estimate for the income row, and a null, both checked.

pathway: Paying families cash rewards tied to school attendance, test scores and health checkups did not raise elementary or middle school test scores.
model_match: Not applicable. Tested model: Opportunity NYC-Family Rewards conditional cash transfers.
typical_effect: No meaningful effects on grade 3-8 math or ELA proficiency; positive Regents or credit effects only for high school students who entered grade 9 as proficient readers.
caveats: Partners offering attendance or achievement incentives to families should not expect test-score effects.
rationale: A large randomized null for a family-incentive model.

pathway: Paying students for test scores or grades did not raise standardized math scores.
model_match: Not applicable. Tested model: cash incentives paid to students for outputs (scores, grades) or inputs (reading books, attendance).
typical_effect: No statistically significant effects on standardized math or reading in Chicago, NYC or DC; incentives for inputs did better than incentives for outputs.
caveats: Relevant to partners that give stipends or prizes for grades or test performance.
rationale: Large randomized null for student incentives.

proposed_tier: not-recommended for S7 and S8 (split from S5 and S6)
pathway: Universal social and emotional learning curricula have not reliably raised state math test scores in large randomized trials.
model_match: Not used for credit for math.
typical_effect: Federal multisite RCT of seven school-delivered programs: no overall academic effect after three years; Chicago Positive Action trial: ISAT math not significant per WWC; recent meta-analysis: math g = 0.08; second-grade effectiveness trial: no effect; INSIGHTS gains faded by middle school.
caveats: PATHS (24 schools) and Positive Action in Hawaii (school-level) report positive state-test results, but they are smaller trials by developers. Older meta-analyses (Durlak 2011, Corcoran 2018 at +0.26 for math) shrink in large rigorous trials. The ELA screener should weigh the same trials for S5 and S6.
rationale: A null at scale (the SACD consortium trial) outweighs positive pilots under the bar; the math part of L-13 should not stay recommended.

evidence_level: B (one lottery-based natural experiment plus two quasi-experiments)
pathway: A full-time school coordinator who reviews every student and links each to tailored services and enrichment raises state math scores by grade 5.
model_match: City Connects model: a full-time coordinator per school conducting a whole-class review of every student each year, individual support plans, and links to community services, sustained three or more years.
typical_effect: MCAS math g = 0.21 (lottery sample, grades 3-5, largest at grade 5); replication site about 0.5 SD after five years of implementation.
caveats: Effects grow with years of exposure, so one- or two-year partnerships should not claim them. The replication uses fixed effects, not a lottery. Generic community schools did not move math (Tennessee; NYC significant only in year 3, see L-38). Developer-affiliated evaluators. Plan on about 0.2 SD, not 0.5.
rationale: The one integrated-support model with lottery-based state math evidence; the map lists it only for dropout (L-40).

pathway: Community schools and case-management models in general have not moved state math scores.
model_match: Not used for credit (see the City Connects proposal for the one model that has).
typical_effect: Tennessee community schools: no change in math, small ELA gain, more chronic absence; Communities In Schools of Kalamazoo: only attendance affected; Massachusetts Wraparound Zones: better state test performance (size to check).
caveats: Harlem Children's Zone: community programs without the charter school were not associated with achievement gains. Keep the generic row not recommended.
rationale: More evidence that the generic community-school label earns no math credit.

pathway: Schools partnered with an AmeriCorps near-peer service corps were more likely to raise proficiency rates, but the only evidence is a school-level comparison commissioned by the program.
model_match: Not applicable. Model: City Year Whole School Whole Child.
typical_effect: Partner schools two to three times more likely to increase ELA and math proficiency; about one month of added learning.
caveats: School-level, funder-commissioned, no student-level comparison; City Year operates in Philadelphia, so partners will cite it. Contrast with Math Corps (L-02), which has student-level RCTs.
rationale: What not to claim for a common Philadelphia partner model.

pathway: Relationship-building teacher home visits showed a small math gain in one matched study and none in a randomized trial.
model_match: Not applicable.
typical_effect: DC matched comparison: DC CAS math g = 0.12 per WWC (confirm); St. Louis cluster RCT: no academic differences.
caveats: The randomized trial had fidelity problems. Home visits have better evidence for attendance and discipline (L-32, S1).
rationale: Mixed evidence; not enough for math credit.

pathway: Family math activities at home (apps, interactive homework, summer packets) have not shown reliable gains on standardized math tests.
model_match: Not applicable.
typical_effect: Bedtime Math app: g = 0.07, not significant per WWC; online home summer math: no effect; TIPS interactive math homework: positive standardized math in one study of 153 students.
caveats: TIPS is very low cost and worth a replication by a partner with a comparison group, but one small study is not enough.
rationale: Low-cost family math ideas partners propose; shows which have been tested and how far.

pathway: Automated messages to parents about grades and missed work raise grades, but barely move standardized math scores.
model_match: Not applicable.
typical_effect: U.S. trial: Smarter Balanced math g = -0.01 (GPA +0.11); English secondary trial: maths +0.03.
caveats: Consistent with the existing row: messaging moves effort and grades more than tests.
rationale: Replication.

pathway: School-based and monitoring-style mentoring did not raise state math test scores in national and city randomized trials.
model_match: Not applicable.
typical_effect: Federal Student Mentoring Program RCT: no effect on state math proficiency; Check & Connect RCT: no test-score effects (attendance gains in grades 5-7); school-based mentoring meta-analysis: very small effects.
caveats: Mentoring may help attendance (S1); it should not be credited for math.
rationale: Adds the national randomized null for state math.

pathway: Brief growth-mindset and affirmation exercises have not raised standardized or end-of-course math scores.
model_match: Not applicable.
typical_effect: Meta-analysis: very small or null achievement effects after quality and bias adjustment; Texas self-affirmation trial: no STAAR end-of-course effect; implicit-theories trial: no change in Algebra I D grades; Philadelphia-area affirmation trial: failed replication.
caveats: The national mindset study raised grade 9 math grades by about 0.05 SD, a grade, not a test. Complements L-21 (values affirmation, Y5) and L-91 (self-concept, associated).
rationale: Low-cost classroom exercises partners propose; the test-score evidence is null.

pathway: School eye exams and free glasses give a small, fading gain on state reading and math tests.
model_match: Not applicable.
typical_effect: Florida cluster RCT: about 2 percentage points higher chance of passing the state math and reading tests, fading over time.
caveats: Second randomized trial in the same direction as Neitzel 2021; still small and short-lived.
rationale: Replication with a state-test outcome.

pathway: After-school exercise and physically active lessons did not significantly change math achievement in randomized trials.
model_match: Not applicable.
typical_effect: After-school aerobic exercise RCT: broad math g = 0.09 to 0.30, not significant; three-year active-lessons RCT: no academic effect (and no harm).
caveats: Useful 'no harm' finding: active time does not cost achievement.
rationale: Two more randomized nulls.

pathway: Music and arts participation does not raise math scores once prior differences between participants and others are controlled.
model_match: Not applicable.
typical_effect: National datasets with propensity weighting or prior-achievement controls: no effect on math (ECLS-K, ELS SAT, HSLS:09).
caveats: A 2025 meta-analysis reports g = 0.36 for music interventions on math, but it conflicts with Sala & Gobet and likely includes weak designs; check before citing.
rationale: Strengthens the arts null for math and flags the conflicting meta-analysis.

pathway: More days in school cause higher math scores in the middle grades.
model_match: Same as L-27: school-record attendance gains for the partner's own students against a comparison group.
typical_effect: Consistent negative effects of absences on math across instrumental-variables (school nurse availability), student fixed effects (California) and longitudinal (Chicago) designs.
caveats: Magnitude note: the attendance gains found for 21st CCLC (about 0.5 to 3 days) imply under 0.01 SD on math through this pathway. Partners should not stack an attendance claim and a direct math claim for the same students.
rationale: Independent designs agree; adds a magnitude check that ties the 21st CCLC attendance results to math.

pathway: More absences, especially unexcused ones, are associated with lower grade 3-4 math scores in Philadelphia.
model_match: Not applicable.
typical_effect: Philadelphia grades 2-4 with student fixed effects: unexcused absences more strongly negative than excused.
caveats: Second Philadelphia study by the same author; independent of the SDP slide deck.
rationale: Adds a Philadelphia longitudinal study to the grade 3 associated row.

proposed_tier: not-recommended for partner credit (unchanged); B for math teacher PD
pathway: Sustained math professional development on formative assessment and student learning progressions raises students' math achievement.
model_match: Not used for partner credit unless the partner is the PD provider. Tested model: OGAP-style formative-assessment PD with school-based routines, grades 3-5; state-funded K-3 math intervention grants with coaching.
typical_effect: OGAP cluster RCT, 61 Philadelphia-area schools: meaningful impacts on student math (size and test to check); Kentucky Math Achievement Fund: gains in math, reading and attendance.
caveats: Relevant to intermediary and PD partners, not to direct-service youth programs.
rationale: A Philadelphia-area randomized math PD result the map does not have.

evidence_level: Suggestive: one RCT; one QE null
pathway: Career and technical education teachers who work with math teachers to make the math in their trade explicit raise students' standardized math scores.
model_match: Math-in-CTE: CTE teachers paired with math teachers, intensive PD, and math-enhanced lessons embedded in the CTE course.
typical_effect: Significantly higher on two of three standardized math tests (TerraNova, ACCUPLACER) after one year; technical skills unchanged.
caveats: One RCT of volunteer teachers; a later quasi-experiment of integrated units found reading but not math gains on a state test. Not the Keystone.
rationale: A low-cost practice change for CTE partners that touches Algebra I content.

pathway: Online algebra credit recovery left students with lower algebra scores and fewer recovered credits than face-to-face credit recovery.
model_match: Not applicable. Tested contrast: online vs face-to-face summer Algebra I credit recovery for ninth graders who failed.
typical_effect: Online students less likely to recover credit and scored lower on an algebra posttest (1,224 students, 17 Chicago high schools).
caveats: Practical guidance: partners running credit recovery should keep a teacher in the room. The companion study of expanding summer credit recovery should be checked for its own effects.
rationale: A randomized result directly about Algebra I that partners can act on.

evidence_level: Suggestive: one cluster RCT outside the US
pathway: A program that rewards children with credits for attending after-school clubs, visits and volunteering raised maths attainment slightly.
model_match: Children's University: local teams organize 30 or more hours a year of extracurricular activities with credits, certificates and a graduation event (ages 9-11).
typical_effect: About two additional months' progress in Key Stage 2 maths (moderate security) and reading.
caveats: England, efficacy trial; children volunteered, so the comparison is among volunteers; no US replication.
rationale: A low-cost recognition structure that could layer onto existing after-school offerings; listed as suggestive only.

evidence_level: B for credits; C for math
pathway: A whole-ninth-grade model of teacher teams and weekly relationship lessons raises credits and grades, with inconsistent effects on math test scores.
model_match: Not used for partner credit. Tested model: BARR school-wide ninth-grade model.
typical_effect: Student-level RCT (11 schools): NWEA math significantly higher; validation RCT: NWEA math g = 0.01, not significant; scale-up: math test result to check; Evidence for ESSA math mean +0.09.
caveats: A school-run model; partners can support but not run it. Better evidence for on-track (S4) than for math.
rationale: Several screeners will see BARR; this records the math part as inconsistent.
